video.title: Success is Hard Until You Understand This Formula

summary: Codie Sanchez explains her 'AOV to CAC' formula: judge a business by first-order average order value against full customer acquisition cost, rather than lifetime value, which she argues is usually miscalculated and leads to burning cash. She covers raising AOV through value-based pricing (10-20% of value created) and by adding tiers, subscriptions, upsells and referrals, using a plumber example and her own Boardroom ladder. She then covers lowering CAC with owned demand (organic, referrals, partnerships, email) versus rented paid ads, and gives her media business's return on content spend. The takeaway is to aim for a 3:1 AOV:CAC ratio and check it weekly.

tactics.name: AOV-to-CAC ratio check
steps: Use first-order AOV, not projected LTV
Compute CAC = all acquisition spend incl. ads, marketing and sales labour / net new customers
Target AOV:CAC of 3:1; fix if CAC > half of AOV
Recompute weekly because CAC creeps up ~5% at a time

quote.text: If your CAC is more than half your AOV, then your CAC is not an ratio we like
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

tactics.name: Value-based pricing
steps: Estimate dollar value created or disaster avoided
Price at 10-20% of value created
Answer 'too expensive' with 'compared to what?' and the avoided cost

tactics.name: Increase customer surface area
steps: Add checklist inspection upsell
Add premium/priority subscription tier
Cross-sell partner services for referral fees
Build three tiers: free/low cost, speed and depth, full access; add the top tier only when tier two is full

tactics.name: Owned demand percentage
steps: Sum revenue from organic, referrals and partnerships
Divide by total revenue
Aim above 50% so growth does not depend on ad algorithms

tactics.name: Return on content spend (ROCS)
steps: Audience value = revenue per channel / followers
Multiply by frequency and lifetime
Divide by content spend

tactics.name: Channel sequencing by revenue stage
steps: Under $250k: master one channel
$250k-$1M: add a second (organic then test paid)
$1M-$5M: run two or three with at least one owned
Over $5M: any channel, keep majority of budget on proven ones

warnings.warning: Losing money on the first sale while banking on LTV only works with VC money; most businesses go bankrupt doing it.

lessons.lesson: Judge acquisition against first-order value, not projected lifetime value.

quote.text: if you're profitable on the first order, you never need a projection to save you
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

lessons.lesson: Raise prices: small increases flow almost entirely to profit.
Price to the outcome or disaster avoided, not the time taken.

quote.text: We don't want to price ourselves based on our input. We want to price it based on their desired outcome
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

lessons.lesson: Low prices often reflect a lack of confidence in what you sell.

quote.text: your lack of confidence shows up in your prices
quote.speaker: Codie Sanchez

lessons.lesson: Sell more to the same customer via tiers, subscriptions, upsells, cross-sells and affiliate referrals.
Include sales and marketing labour in CAC to see real survival economics.
Owned attention (email, followers, SEO) has a long tail; ads stop when spending stops.
Email remains the highest-ROI marketing channel.
Master one channel before adding more; sequence by revenue stage.

evidence_quality.rationale: Mostly framework teaching with cited statistics. Her own revenue and member-ROI figures are first-hand but unverified. The transcript has misheard words (CAP/cash for CAC, rocks for ROCS, JBLIS for JVs).
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Promotes her new book, Boardroom ($24k/yr) with advisor sales calls, Exit Ready advisory, and a free live event with prizes.

extraction.review_notes: The extraction is solid and faithful to this framework-heavy promotional tutorial. Ideas, the plumber example and the media-business figures are captured accurately. The main issues are a garbled merged claim about organic vs paid brands, a few missed benchmark stats, and an overly generous acquisition automation score for an advisor-call-led coaching sale. The C rating is appropriate given the heavy self-promotion and unverified self-reported numbers.
